items.item: A duplicate-rejected error and an out-of-sequence error look similar on the surface but mean opposite things: the first is safe and expected, the second signals real data loss.

at.step: Reveal: anything but the very next number bounces off

items.item: The per-partition scoping of the sequence counter is what lets a single idempotent producer write to many partitions in parallel without any of them blocking on another's counter.

at.step: Reveal: every partition's counter starts its own story

items.item: A zombie producer isn't necessarily malicious or buggy — it's often just a previous, still-finishing instance of the exact same honest producer after a routine restart.

at.step: Reveal: a restart fences out whatever got left behind

items.item: This topic's epoch mechanism is a smaller-scope cousin of the leader-epoch fencing from the replication topic — both use a bumped counter to invalidate a stale actor's stale state.

at.step: Reveal: a restart fences out whatever got left behind

items.item: Idempotence closes exactly the first of the two crash windows named in the previous topic; the second (a consumer crash between processing and offset commit) is untouched by anything this topic does.

at.step: Hook: the same retry, with a rejection now in the way

items.item: Two producers both writing a logically identical record each get their own producer id, so idempotence provides zero protection against that specific duplication source.

at.step: Reveal: exactly this wide, and no wider

items.item: An application that needs duplicate protection across a producer restart must supply its own stable identity (an event id, a business key) rather than relying on the broker-assigned producer id, which changes on every restart.

at.step: Reveal: exactly this wide, and no wider

items.item: The toy model's three checks are independent of each other by construction: duplicate rejection, cross-partition independence, and epoch fencing each test a different axis of the same mechanism.

at.step: Prove it

items.item: Multi-partition atomicity — making several of these per-partition writes succeed or fail together as one unit — needs a mechanism this topic deliberately doesn't build, since it's the next topic's entire subject.

The precision of this topic's scope statement (one producer, one session, one partition) is itself the main lesson — a vaguer claim like 'idempotent producers prevent duplicates' would be actively misleading.
